1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
13	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
14	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
15	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
16	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
17	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
18	
19	## How to commit
20	
21	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
22	
23	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
24	
25	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
26	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
27	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
28	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
29	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
30	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
31	
32	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
33	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
34	
35	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
36	
37	## Pushing
38	
39	Push after every commit.
40	
41	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
42	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
43	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
44	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
45	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
46	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
47	
48	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
53

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

## B.13 Where each library enters

Interpreter: `default_library` is `AnyType`, `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:48-49,128-137`); the sources are found on `fortress.source.path`, which is `.` then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` then `Library` then `ProjectFortress/test_library` (`default_repository/configuration:44`); they enter as graph roots (`GraphRepository.java:125-165`) and are analysed through the same phase chain as the user program, then linked by `Driver.evalComponent` (`interpreter/Driver.java:140-162`).

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	A generic function passed as a value takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it: a parameter, a local variable declared with the type, or an assignment. So `app(half, v)` runs for `half[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): Vector[\RR64,n\]` and `app(f: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\], v: Vector[\RR64,3\])`. Where no arrow type receives it, or the arrow type leaves a static parameter open, the value stays generic. Walk then infers the static arguments at each application. The checker refuses such a program, so do not rely on this in a program for both paths (ledger row 1021). Walk departs from this in three cases:
17	
18	- An immutable top-level variable of arrow type, an object's field of arrow type and a declared arrow return type keep the generic value. So for a top-level `g: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\] = half`, `g(w)` runs for a `w: Vector[\RR64,2\]` (ledger rows 1019, 1036).
19	- For `appT[\T\](f: T -> T, x: T)`, `appT(half, v)` is refused, 'Unification error': `v` fixes `T` by its run-time type. Write the static argument, as `appT(half[\3\], v)` (ledger row 1018).
20	- A generic function declared inside a block stops at its declaration, whether it is passed or not: 'Missing type T' (ledger row 1020). Declare it at the top level.
21	
22	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
23	
24	Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.
25	
26	- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
27	- A numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, not to its default. So `a = 0` is `true` for `a: Any` that holds a zero `NN32`, where the rules' answer is `false` (ledger row 1016). To compare as the rules do, bind the numeral first, as `z = 0`, then write `a = z`.
28	- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
29	- A numeral type written in a `comprises` clause loads and runs, as `trait T comprises { NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\] } end` does (ledger row 981). The rules refuse it, as the compiled checker does, and as walk does at load in an `extends` clause or as a static argument: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
30	- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.
31	
32	Walk also departs from the rules at these bindings:
33	
34	- A `var` declared in a block with an array type and bound to an array literal, as `var t: ZZ32[2] = [5 6]`, is immutable: 'Cannot assign to immutable t' (ledger row 1024). Bind the literal to an immutable name, and initialize the `var` from it.
35	- An array literal assigned to a variable, as `t := [7 8]`, is not built into an array: 'Type mismatch assigning' (ledger row 1025). Bind the literal to an immutable name of the array type, and assign the name.
36	
37	## Where a fix of walk belongs
38	
39	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
40	
41	- coercion;
42	- chained comparisons;
43	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
44	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
45	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
46	
47	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
48	
49	Walk keeps each choice of a declaration in a dispatch cache, except a choice that asked a program's own type for its numeral coercion: that coercion's `where` clause can take one numeral and refuse another. If you change how a numeral chooses a declaration, check that the cache's key (`Numerals.Keys`) tells apart the calls that now choose differently.
50	
51	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
52	
53	## What walk checks
54	
55	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiled path's desugaring switches, and the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So by default `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program. With the variable, it checks the program against walk's library, but after the compiled path's desugarings. `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
56	
57	Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
58	
59	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
60	
61	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
62	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
63	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
64	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
65	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
66	
67	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
68	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
69	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
70	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
71	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
72	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
73	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
74	  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
75	  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
76	  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
77	  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
78	  - Beside a generic declaration, it does not judge by the Return Type Rule a declaration without static parameters that writes no return type and whose parameter types are object types, as the number types other than `QQ` are: `pick[\T extends Number\](a: T): ZZ32 = 1` beside `pick(a: NN32) = "two"` loads (ledger row 1044). Write the return type.
79	  - It reads no `comprises` clause for the Return Type Rule. So it refuses a valid pair over a program's own trait that comprises one object, as `pickFirst[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): T` beside `pickFirst(a: Mine, b: Mine): Mine`, where `Mine` extends `Number` and comprises one object.
80	  - It refuses a valid pair where the generic declaration's result is a tuple that holds its type parameter, as `pt[\T extends Number\](a: T): (T, ZZ32)` beside `pt(a: RR64): (RR64, ZZ32)`: 'fails the Return Type Rule' (ledger row 1058).
81	  - It reads two parameter lists as excluding where, in one of them, every parameter at which the two differ is an object type, even an object below the other list's type there. So `f(x: Number): ZZ32` beside `f(x: ZZ64): String` loads, which the checker refuses (ledger row 697).
82	  - It loads two generic dotted methods of one name that differ in their number of parameters, as `tk[\U\](y: U, z: U)` beside `tk[\U\](y: U, z: U, w: U)`. A call then fails with 'Cannot find definition for method' (ledger row 1057). Give the two methods two names.
83	  - It loads a pair that breaks the Return Type Rule over an arrow type, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle -> Circle): (Circle -> Circle)`: a function of type `Any -> Circle` is also a `Circle -> Circle`, and at that instance the generic one returns `Any -> Circle`. The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 1049).
84	
85	  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
86	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
87	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
88	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
89	- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
90	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
91	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
92	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
93	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
94	
95	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
96	
97	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
98	
99	- adds an overload;
100	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
101	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
102	- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`;
103	- names, in a `builtinPrimitive` string, a helper that walk refuses ("Natives").
104	
105	Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.
106	
107	Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.
108	
109	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
110	
111	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
112	
113	## Natives
114	
115	The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:
116	
117	- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
118	- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
119	
120	Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:
121	
122	- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
123	- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.
124	
125	In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method: a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own.
126	
127	A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.
128	
129	Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:
130	
131	- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
132	- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
133	- The binding is in a method of a type whose `self` walk does not carry, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
134	- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list above, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.
135	
136	The check has two gaps:
137	
138	- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
139	- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `JavaBufferedWriter` loads. A call of its inherited native method then stops with 'No Java FortressBufferedWriter carries' and the object's name (ledger row 928). Extend `WriteStream`, the library's trait of an output stream (`Library/Stream.fsi`), instead.
140	
141	A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. A `||` of string literals folds into one literal, a `FlatString`, so a test that needs a `CatString` joins a literal with a variable. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.
142	
143	An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.
144	
145	A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `ZZ32.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:
146	
147	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
148	    return new FortressError(f);
149	
150	A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string is the exception's simple name, and `compiler/runtimeValues/LibraryNames.java` maps it to the class of the compiled library in use (`compiler.md`, "The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over"). Under walk, no class of a compiled library loads, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.
151	
152	## Running a program
153	
154	    bin/fortress P.fss
155	
156	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
157	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
158	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
159	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
160	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
161	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
162	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

164	## The model program
165	
166	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
167	
168	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
169	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

junit.sh
#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then

content.content:
## The ladder regression

The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:

- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.

A file that moved gets a mark:

- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
- MISSING: a file with no output.
- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.

DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.

To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:

1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt

2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.

If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.

## Comparing with an earlier run

- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.

# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

(* AplCore -- the library half of the APL sub-language: the redesign of v1/base,
   promoted to the base on 2026-09-13.  APL's values are Fortress's
   own arrays: a scalar is an RR64, a vector an Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], a matrix an
   Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] (merged ledger row 57).  There is NO wrapper type
   and no runtime rank field: every primitive is an overload family whose
   PARAMETERS are RR64 / Vector[\RR64,s\] / Matrix[\RR64,r,c\] -- the only
   spelling on which Fortress will overload by rank, because Vector and Matrix
   reach the mutually excluding Rank1 and Rank2 while two instantiations of
   Array[\E,I\] do not exclude each other (r01_native.out, r02a_rankover.out).
   Results are the honest runtime-sized Array[\...\] types.

   Operators, not names, wherever the glyph is in the host operator table
   (Specification/appendices/operators.tex) -- and a top-level opr DOES cross
   an api boundary (r03_apiopr.out), which sharpens merged ledger row 30.
   Index origin 0. *)
api AplCore

(* numbers and formatting *)
aplInt(v: RR64): ZZ32
aplNegS(v: RR64): RR64
aplFmt(v: RR64): String
aplPad(s: String, w: ZZ32): String

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

content.content:
\seclabel{shadowing}

In this section,
we define the \emph{reach} and \emph{scope} of a declaration,
which determine where a declared name may be used to refer to the entity
declared by the declaration.  
It is a static error 
for a reference to a name to occur at any point in a program
at which the name is not \emph{in scope} in the appropriate namespace
(as defined below),
except immediately after the `.'
of a dotted field access or dotted method invocation
when the name is the name of the field or dotted method
if the declaration is a labeled block,
any point in a \KWD{spawn} expression
in the labeled block.

\end{itemize}
We say that a name is \emph{in scope} in a namespace 
at any point in the program 
that is in the scope of some declaration for that name and namespace.
Again, we omit the name and/or namespace when they are clear from context.

As mentioned above,
it is a static error for a reference to a name to occur 
where it is not in scope in the appropriate namespace.
In addition, 
local variables must be properly initialized before they are used, 
as discussed in \chapref{variables}.
99:\section{Kinds of Declarations}
354:\section{Namespaces}
408:\section{Reach and Scope of Declarations}

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason

content.content:
analysed ASTs, walk's rewritten ASTs and environments, compiled jars,
       native wrappers.  Fortress checks an entry against its Fortress sources,
       by date, and never against the implementation, so the build decides
       whether the caches still belong to the implementation:
       - ${build}/implementation.stamp is a SHA-1 over the implementation as it
         runs: every file of ${build}, ${buildOne}, ${PF}/third_party and bin, and
         default_repository/configuration, each with its relative path, and
         the JDK's version.  compileAll writes it last, after a successful
         build, and deletes it first.
       - A caches folder holds the stamp of the implementation it belongs to.
         At its end, compileAll keeps a caches folder only if that stamp equals
         the new build's: the implementation is byte for byte the one that
         filled it.  Otherwise it deletes the folder and starts it again, empty,
         with the new stamp.
       - ${build}/implementation.sources is a SHA-1 over what the build is made
         from: ${PF}/src (class files aside), ${PF}/src-one, ${PF}/astgen, ${PF}/third_party,
         bin, build.xml and default_repository/configuration, and the JDK's
         version.  When it differs at the start of compileAll, the build may
         change the implementation, so the caches are deleted before anything
         compiles, as cleanCache did here before: a build that then fails
         leaves no caches behind.  So are they when the build directory is no
         longer what the last build left (something else compiled into it).
       - scalac runs only when its inputs (the sources) or the build directory
         differ from what the last successful build left; for the same inputs
         its output is the same, byte for byte.
       ant cleanCache deletes the caches whatever their stamp; ant clean
       deletes the build too.
  -->

       with the JDK's version, into the property @{property}. -->
  <macrodef name="fingerprint">
    <attribute name="property"/>
    <element name="files" implicit="yes"/>
    <sequential>
      <delete dir="${build}/.fingerprint" quiet="true"/>
      <checksum algorithm="SHA-1" todir="${build}/.fingerprint"
                totalproperty="@{property}.sha1" forceoverwrite="yes">
        <files/>
      </checksum>
      <delete dir="${build}/.fingerprint" quiet="true"/>
      <property name="@{property}"
                value="${@{property}.sha1} java ${java.runtime.version}"/>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>
  <!-- What the build is made from. -->
  <macrodef name="sourcesFingerprint">
    <attribute name="property"/>
    <sequential>
      <fingerprint property="@{property}">
        <fileset dir="${basedir}">
          <include name="${PF}/src/**"/>

## What changed and why

Two lines in each of the one library's api and component, after `opr <->`:

    Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793  opr EQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean
    Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2794  opr NEQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean

    Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4924  opr NEQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean = NOT (a EQV b)

The parser reads `EQV`, `EQUIV` and `≡` as one operator, U+2261, and `NEQV` and `≢` as U+2262 (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Literal.rats:301-306`). The specification gives `≡` on booleans: "returns true if both arguments are true or both arguments are false" (`Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:256-258`), and `≢` as `¬` of `≡` (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:33-34`). The one library's boolean operators are top-level operators over two booleans; the two join them in that form (fork E1), and the prelude gains nothing (P-37).

### Why walk failed two ways on the base

`≡` is a chaining operator, so the parser builds `t ≡ t` as a `ChainExpr`. Walk turns the chain desugaring off (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:286-288`, `:491-492`), and the disambiguator checks the operator of an `OpExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:497-503`) but not a chain's links. So the undeclared `≡` loads, and `forChainExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:437-469`) calls `getOp` (`:893-909`), which raises the bug for the unresolved reference. `≢` is not a chaining operator: it stays an `OpExpr`, which the disambiguator refuses before the run, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' The compiled path desugars the chain first (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/PreDisambiguationDesugarer.java:96-97`), so its disambiguator refuses both. In the analysed tree of a probe, the `≡` link's `OpRef` has `_lexicalDepth=-2147483648` inside a `ChainExpr` (`tmp/` probe, `EqvOnlyProbe`).

## Findings

1. **The one library declares the logical equivalence of two booleans, `EQV` (`≡`, U+2261), and its negation `NEQV` (`≢`, U+2262), as top-level operators over two booleans beside `opr <->`** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793-2794`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923-4924`). `EQV`'s body is `if a then b else NOT b end`, which calls no `=`; `NEQV`'s is `NOT (a EQV b)`, the specification's definition (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:34-35`). ### Why walk failed two ways on the base

`≡` is a chaining operator, so the parser builds `t ≡ t` as a `ChainExpr`. Walk turns the chain desugaring off (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:286-288`, `:491-492`), and the disambiguator checks the operator of an `OpExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:498-503`) but not a chain's links. So the undeclared `≡` loads, and `forChainExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:437-469`) calls `getOp` (`:893-909`), which raises the bug for the unresolved reference. `≢` is not a chaining operator: it stays an `OpExpr`, which the disambiguator refuses before the run, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' The compiled path desugars the chain first (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/PreDisambiguationDesugarer.java:96-97`), so its disambiguator refuses both. In the analysed tree of a probe, the `≡` link's `OpRef` has `_lexicalDepth=-2147483648` inside a `ChainExpr` (`tmp/` probe, `EqvOnlyProbe`).
